```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fit_stateful = TRUE)
source(system.file("knitr/fit-cache.R", package = "tulpa"))
```


A nested Laplace fit solves one inner problem per cell of its hyperparameter
grid, and a NUTS fit runs several independent chains. Either can run for
hours, and a reboot or a killed job near the end would otherwise lose all of
it. With `control$checkpoint` set, tulpa appends every finished cell or chain
to a file; a later call with the same inputs loads what is finished and
computes only the rest. This article turns checkpointing on, cuts the file
the way a kill during a write would, resumes from it, and shows the file
being refused once the data change.

Installation is covered in [Get started](tulpa.html).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## Turn it on

`control$checkpoint = list(path =, resume =)` takes the file and whether to
continue from it. With a `path` given, `resume` defaults to `TRUE`;
`resume = FALSE` removes any existing file and starts over. The example is a
binomial model with an intrinsic CAR field on a chain of 30 regions, fitted
by nested Laplace through `mode = "structured"`. `fit_ckpt()` wraps the call
so the later sections can repeat it with other data or another `resume`.

```{r fit, fit = c("df", "ckpt", "fit_ckpt", "fit", "full_size")}
set.seed(20260716)
S <- 30L
W <- matrix(0, S, S)
for (i in 1:(S - 1)) W[i, i + 1] <- W[i + 1, i] <- 1
df <- data.frame(region = factor(seq_len(S)))
df$x <- as.integer(df$region) / 10 + rnorm(S, 0, 0.3)
df$y <- rbinom(S, 20, plogis(-0.4 + 0.5 * df$x))

ckpt <- tempfile(fileext = ".ckpt")
fit_ckpt <- function(data, resume) {
  tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region), data = data, family = "binomial",
        n_trials = rep(20L, S), spatial = spatial_car(W, level = "obs"),
        mode = "structured",
        control = list(n_threads = 2,
                       checkpoint = list(path = ckpt, resume = resume)))
}
fit <- fit_ckpt(df, resume = FALSE)
coef(fit)
full_size <- file.size(ckpt)
full_size
```

The file starts with a header holding a fingerprint of the inputs: the
response, trial counts, design matrix, offsets, the field's structure and the
solver settings. Each solved grid cell follows as one record, keyed by its
hyperparameter coordinate and closed by a checksum over key and payload.

## Resume after an interruption

A job killed while it writes leaves a file that ends in the middle of a
record. Cutting the file to 45% of its bytes reproduces that: the records
before the cut are intact, the last one is torn, and the rest are missing.

```{r interrupt, fit = TRUE}
bytes <- readBin(ckpt, "raw", full_size)
writeBin(bytes[seq_len(floor(0.45 * full_size))], ckpt)
file.size(ckpt)
```

The same call with `resume = TRUE` reads the intact records, detects the torn
one by its short length or failed checksum, truncates the file to the last
good record, and solves the cells that are not on disk, appending each as it
finishes.

```{r resume, fit = TRUE}
fit2 <- fit_ckpt(df, resume = TRUE)
c(size_after_resume = file.size(ckpt), size_uninterrupted = full_size)
all.equal(coef(fit), coef(fit2))
```

The file is complete again, and the resumed fit returns the coefficients of
the uninterrupted one.

## A changed input is refused

Resuming onto a file written for other inputs would mix cells from two
models. Changing a single count changes the fingerprint, and the resume
stops before solving anything:

```{r fingerprint, error = TRUE, fit = c("df_changed")}
df_changed <- df
df_changed$y[1] <- df_changed$y[1] + 1L
fit_ckpt(df_changed, resume = TRUE)
```

`resume = FALSE` on the same path discards the old file and fits the new
data from the start:

```{r restart, fit = TRUE}
fit3 <- fit_ckpt(df_changed, resume = FALSE)
coef(fit3)
```

## Sampler chains

The sampler kernel of `mode = "hmc"` takes the same `control$checkpoint`,
with a chain as the unit. A chain is deterministic in its seed, its chain
number, the data and the settings, so a resumed run returns exactly the
draws of the uninterrupted one. The example is a Poisson model with a random
intercept over 10 groups, four chains, cut at 60% of the file:

```{r chains, fit = c("ckpt_chains")}
set.seed(1)
g <- factor(rep(1:10, each = 10))
d <- data.frame(g = g, x = rnorm(100))
d$y <- rpois(100, exp(0.3 + 0.4 * d$x + rnorm(10, 0, 0.5)[g]))

ckpt_chains <- tempfile(fileext = ".ckpt")
fit_chains <- function(resume) {
  tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "poisson", mode = "hmc",
        control = list(n_chains = 4, n_iter = 1000, warmup = 500, seed = 11,
                       checkpoint = list(path = ckpt_chains, resume = resume)))
}
run1 <- fit_chains(resume = FALSE)
size <- file.size(ckpt_chains)
writeBin(readBin(ckpt_chains, "raw", size)[seq_len(floor(0.6 * size))],
         ckpt_chains)
run2 <- fit_chains(resume = TRUE)
identical(run1$draws, run2$draws)
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE, fit = TRUE}
unlink(c(ckpt, ckpt_chains))
```

The records are stored in the byte order of the machine that wrote them, so
a checkpoint is for resuming on that machine, not for moving a fit between
platforms. The
fitters that take `control$checkpoint` are the nested Laplace doors
(`tulpa_nested_laplace()`, `tulpa_nested_laplace_joint()`, `fit_spde()` and
`tulpa()` when it routes to them) and the NUTS/HMC sampler; other sampler
backends refuse the key.
